subject: Anatomy
summary: The clavicle is a curved bone that connects the arm to the trunk, stabilising the shoulder and acting as a strut. Its shape and attachments influence shoulder mechanics and are key in trauma assessment.

sections.p: The clavicle is the longest and most lateral of the thoracic bones, forming the medial part of the shoulder girdle. It bridges the sternum and scapula, providing a rigid yet flexible link that allows a wide range of arm movements while protecting neurovascular structures.

It lies superficially on the superior thoracic wall, extending from the sternoclavicular joint medially to the acromioclavicular joint laterally. The bone has a convex medial surface, a concave lateral surface, and a narrow, flat shaft.

t.b: A displaced fracture indicates need for reduction or surgery

sections.p: Medially, the sternum and mediastinal vessels lie beneath; laterally, the acromion and deltoid muscle overlay. The subclavius muscle and brachial plexus run underneath the clavicle.
The supraclavicular artery and the thoracoacromial artery give off branches that perfuse the clavicle and surrounding tissues.
The brachial plexus roots pass beneath the clavicle; the supraclavicular nerves provide cutaneous sensation over the clavicle.
It stabilises the shoulder, allows arm elevation, and protects neurovascular structures by acting as a lever and a protective shield.

Fractures are common in falls or traffic accidents. Complications include malunion, nonunion, neurovascular injury, and shoulder dysfunction. In low‑resource settings, delayed presentation can lead to chronic disability.
b: Most common fracture in children and adults

sections.p: Remember that a midshaft fracture is the most frequent. A displaced fracture can compress the brachial plexus, causing numbness in the arm. In children, the fracture often remodels, whereas adults may need surgical fixation.

t.b: Loss of sensation or motor function indicates plexus involvement

whenToSeekHelp: Severe pain with inability to move arm

faq.q: What is the most common type of clavicle fracture?
faq.a: The midshaft fracture is the most frequent, accounting for about 70% of all clavicle fractures.

faq.q: Can a clavicle fracture heal on its own?
faq.a: Yes, especially in children and in non‑displaced fractures; the bone remodels well over time.

faq.q: What are the risks of untreated clavicle fractures?
faq.a: Malunion, chronic pain, shoulder dysfunction, and potential neurovascular injury if the fracture is displaced.

exam: Describe the anatomical course of the clavicle and its relevance to shoulder stability.
Explain the clinical approach to a patient with a suspected midshaft clavicle fracture, including key investigations and management options.
Identify the neurovascular structures at risk in a displaced clavicle fracture and explain how to assess for injury.
